text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Special session of parliament celebrated 90 years of universal suffrage in Finland. Finnish women were first in Europe to get the vote.
- Company partly owned by head of the National Board of Taxation suspected of tax fraud.
- The government said in a report to parliament on Tuesday that failure to launch EMU could hurt the European Union. @
- Finnish Broadcasting Company YLE has put its radio news and text television pages on the Internet.
- For young men, the break-up of a romantic affair during military service may lead to serious mental crisis. The army plans to take such cases more seriously.
- KAUPPALEHTI

- The IMF wants Finland to contribute to a reserve fund to be used in case of international financial crisis. Bank of Finland Governor Sirkka Hamalainen says so big sums are involved that issue will need high-level approval. @
- Finnish firms specialised in district heating technology have opportunities for further orders from Sarajevo and other Bosnian cities, says Ekono-Energy Oy executive Risto Seppala.
- British Steel chairman and CEO Sir Brian Moffat says there are too many steel companies in Europe and that the medium-sized firms are unlikely to survive in the long run.
AAMULEHTI
- Finland's Supreme Administrative Court will not take up the case brought against the Office for Free Competition by wholesaler Kesko on its acquisition of rival Tuko. @

- Former minister Marjatta Vaananen says in her memoirs that the Soviet Union tried to buy Centre party women's votes in Finland's 1981 presidential election in return for increased meat purchases by the Soviet Union if the Soviets' favourite candidate, Ahti Karjalainen, got elected.
TURUN SANOMAT

- State-owned power producer Imatran Voima (IVO) considers the expansion of its Naantali coal-fired plant as its most important investment project. Company will not be deterred by Swedish Vattenfall's plans to build plants in Finland. @
- Women members of parliament are generally satisfied with the progress made in equality between the sexes in Finland, but say that equal pay for equal work is still far from reality.
- Finland's oldest citizen, Maija Rothovius, 109 years today. When Mrs. Rothovius was born, Russian Czar Alexander III was grand duke of Finland.
DEMARI
- Finnish breweries says they could create hundreds of new jobs if the beer tax were cut in half.
--Helsinki Newsroom, +358-0-680 50 235
